name: Hawaii under the kapu
title: Social Hierarchy of Hawaii under the Kapu: From Aliʻi Nui to Kauwā
period: 1778–1819 (from Cook's arrival to the end of the kapu)

tiers.name: The paramount chief
tiers.you: You share out the land among your chiefs, you alone may build a war temple, and at the end of each Makahiki you must parry the warriors’ spears to prove yourself worthy to rule.
tiers.kid: Kamehameha I was a great chief who united the Hawaiian Islands and became their first king.
tiers.rise: A ruler usually named a high-born son as his heir, but rivals could take the land by war: Kamehameha overthrew Kalaniʻōpuʻu’s successor Kīwalaʻō in 1782, and Kalanikūpule of Oʻahu, defeated at Nuʻuanu in 1795, was captured and sacrificed to the war god.
tiers.why: Each island kingdom had its paramount chief (aliʻi nui), the greatest of the chiefs in power, if not always in birth.

tiers.name: High chiefs
tiers.term: aliʻi ʻaimoku (district chiefs), nīʻaupiʻo (the highest grade)
tiers.you: You trace your descent from the gods, wear cloaks of red and yellow feathers and govern a district for the ruler, and commoners must not touch your shadow or stand with their heads above yours.
tiers.kid: High chiefs wore cloaks made from many thousands of tiny red and yellow bird feathers.
tiers.rise: Rank came by birth from both parents, so a chief who married a higher-born wife had children who outranked him, while lines that married lower sank. Lands and offices, unlike rank, were won in war: the chiefs who backed Kamehameha after 1782 shared out the lands of the defeated.
tiers.why: The chiefs (aliʻi) traced their descent from the gods, and a chief’s rank depended on the genealogy of both parents.

tiers.name: Lesser chiefs and land agents
tiers.you: You run an ahupuaʻa for your chief: you share out the plots and the water among the farmers and gather their pigs, taro and bark cloth at the Makahiki, but a new chief may bring his own konohiki.
tiers.kid: Konohiki looked after a slice of land for a chief and collected the food and cloth the farmers gave him.
tiers.rise: Lesser chiefs rose by serving a successful chief or by marrying into a higher line, and sank by marrying lower; a konohiki kept his post only as long as his chief held the land.
tiers.why: Below the great chiefs stood the lesser chiefs (kaukaualiʻi), born of a lower-ranking parent, whose lines sank further with every marriage below their rank.

tiers.name: Priests and experts
tiers.you: You are a kahuna: a priest of the gods at a temple, or a master of a craft such as healing or canoe building, trained as an apprentice in your master’s household.
tiers.kid: Kahuna were experts: some were priests, and others were healers, canoe builders or navigators.
tiers.rise: Priestly office often passed from father to son and craft knowledge from master to apprentice, and a kahuna who served a victorious ruler could gain lands. In 1819 Hewahewa himself ordered the images burned and the temples destroyed: the temple priesthood ended, though healers and craftsmen carried on.
tiers.why: A kahuna was an expert, and the word covered priests as well as the masters of a craft or body of knowledge: healers (kahuna lapaʻau), canoe builders, navigators, house builders, genealogists and chanters.

tiers.name: Commoners
tiers.you: You farm taro or fish within an ahupuaʻa, hand part of your harvest and catch to the chief’s konohiki, and must fall face down before a sacred chief; you may move to another chief’s land.
tiers.kid: Most Hawaiians were farmers and fishers who grew taro, caught fish and gave part of their food to the chiefs.
tiers.rise: Commoners were born to their rank and could not become chiefs, though the child of a high chief and a commoner counted as a chief of low grade (aliʻi noanoa). A family could move to another chief’s land, but not out of its class.
tiers.why: Most Hawaiians were commoners (makaʻāinana), who farmed, fished and practised the simpler crafts.

tiers.name: Outcasts
tiers.you: You are kauwā, set apart and despised: you work for the chiefs, no one of a higher class may marry you, and you may be taken as a sacrifice at a war temple.
tiers.kid: The kauwā were outcasts: other Hawaiians were forbidden to marry them, and they worked for the chiefs.
tiers.rise: There was no known way out: kauwā status passed from parents to children, and marriage outside the group was forbidden.
tiers.why: At the bottom stood the kauwā, a hereditary group set apart from every other class and despised by it.
